title: CDR Structure: Career Episodes, CPD, Summary
description: Understand the three parts of a CDR, the career episodes, the CPD list and the summary statement, and how they fit together.

data.sub: Three parts, one connected story of your engineering work.

data.intro: A CDR is easier to write once you see how its three parts support each other.

sections.heading: 1. CPD List
paragraphs: The CPD list records how you have kept your engineering knowledge current: courses, training, seminars, self-study and similar activities.
bullets: Give dates, titles and a short description
Include only activities you can evidence
Keep entries relevant to your engineering field

sections.heading: 2. Career Episodes
paragraphs: You write three career episodes. Each one covers a project or period of work and explains the engineering problem, your own role and the result.
Write in the first person. Say what you did, not what the team did.
sections.note: Check the current Engineers Australia booklet for length and formatting rules before you finish.

sections.heading: 3. Summary Statement
paragraphs: The summary statement is a table that points to the exact paragraphs in your episodes that show each competency element. It helps the assessor find your evidence quickly.

sections.heading: How the Parts Fit
paragraphs: Your episodes provide the evidence, your CPD list shows ongoing learning, and the summary statement connects the evidence to the standard. A gap in one part weakens the others.

items.q: Should all three career episodes cover the same project?
items.a: No. Each episode should describe a different project or period so that together they show a broad range of your engineering work.

items.q: Why must career episodes be in the first person?
items.a: The assessor needs to see your personal contribution. Writing in the first person makes your own role clear and separates it from the team's work.

data.heading: Want an expert to check yours?
data.text: Get clear feedback on structure, depth and competency coverage.
